planting.note: Scatter seed directly on bare, lean soil at the start of the fall rainy season and press in lightly without covering; resents transplanting.

directions: Bowl-shaped wine-red to pink flowers with a distinctive central spot support roughly a hundred native bee species, and this clarkia tolerates heavier clay soils better than most of its relatives, widening its garden applicability. Its tolerance of slow-draining soil makes it one of the more forgiving Clarkia for valley-floor gardens rather than pure decomposed-granite slopes. Thin seedlings to reduce competition if a dense wildflower-mix look isn't wanted, otherwise let it self-sow for a naturalized stand.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into fast, medium, or slow-draining soil; water sparingly after germination to avoid fungal rot in the thin stems.

directions: Large, cup-shaped pink-to-purple blooms with a vivid red center give this clarkia strong visual impact, and it is deer resistant with good container performance. Its central Coast Ranges origin makes it a strong choice for Bay Area and coastal fog-belt gardens where many showier annuals struggle with cool summer nights. It is one of the more soil-flexible Clarkia species, tolerating a range of drainage conditions.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall under open-canopy oaks or Douglas-fir where dappled light and leaf-litter mulch mimic its native understory; avoid clay soil.

directions: Unique reflexed, ribbon-like red sepals pair with white-streaked, three-lobed pink petals, making this one of the few Clarkia genuinely suited to shaded woodland gardens rather than open sun beds. It needs fast-draining duff-like soil and performs poorly in heavy clay. Because it tolerates more shade than nearly any other Clarkia, it fills a specific under-tree niche in native plant gardens that full-sun species cannot.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into sandy, fast-draining soil on a bluff-top or dune-mimicking bed within coastal fog influence; let the decumbent stems sprawl rather than staking.

directions: A genuinely different growth form within the genus, this clarkia's prostrate, decumbent habit makes it useful as a low groundcover-style wildflower for coastal gardens and dune-stabilization plantings, unlike the erect habit of most Clarkia. It is ecologically restricted to coastal bluffs and stabilized dunes, so it is best suited to true coastal gardens within fog influence. Pair it with other Northern Coastal Scrub natives rather than inland wildflower mixes, where it is unlikely to thrive.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, fast-to-slow draining soil; source only the widespread straight species or common subspecies, never the rare federally endangered Pismo clarkia subspecies.

directions: Large fan-shaped petals with a bold red spot create strong visual contrast and attract the uncommon Small Apollo butterfly along with bees, adding pollinator-garden value beyond typical Clarkia. It tolerates a wider soil-drainage range than many of its relatives, suiting Central Coast or Sierra-foothill-style gardens. Its large red-spotted blooms make it a strong substitute where gardeners want farewell-to-spring color but already grow the more common species.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in woodland-edge conditions with light shade from deciduous trees; tolerates colder winter nights than coastal Clarkia species.

directions: Large lavender petals with a contrasting white zone and purple spot support a notably high pollinator count, roughly 86 native bee species, making this an underused Sierra foothill clarkia with strong pollinator-garden value. Being adapted to Sierra foothill woodlands and forests, it tolerates colder winter nights than coastal Clarkia species and suits inland foothill gardens too cold for coastal relatives. Its taller, more erect habit suits it to the back of a native wildflower border rather than front-edge plantings.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into chaparral-margin or woodland-edge conditions with good drainage; avoid rich garden soil, which encourages leggy growth at the expense of flowering.

directions: Distinctive two-lobed petal tips, unique among common garden Clarkia, combine with a tall, almost shrubby annual habit to give strong vertical structure in a wildflower border, and the species serves as a larval host for the Clark's Day Sphinx Moth. Because of its height, give it some support from surrounding plants or a sheltered spot, since the slender stems can flop in wind once flowering. Source straight-species or common-subspecies seed, not wild material of the rarer Mariposa or Brandegee's clarkia subspecies.

planting.note: Direct sow nursery- or seed-bank-sourced seed in fall into grassland or hill conditions mimicking its Monterey-San Benito native range; never wild-collect, given its rarity.

directions: A genuinely rare, narrowly endemic species found only in Monterey and San Benito Counties, this clarkia carries the characteristic pendant-bud-and-fused-sepal display of the genus, valuable for regional native-plant collections and conservation-minded gardens. Commercial seed availability is limited compared to its more common relatives, so source only from nurseries or seed banks that propagate it responsibly. Best suited to specialist native-plant or conservation gardens rather than general wildflower mixes, given its rarity and limited horticultural trade presence.
